Replacing the current list keeps the template\'s sliders (g, v₀…) from clashing with yours. Adding keeps both, but the same name may be defined twice.
v₀ = launch speed (m/s), α = launch angle (degrees), g = gravity. The middle point is the greatest height H, the last is the range R. The range is largest at α = 45°.
x is time t, y is velocity v = u + at. The area under the line is the displacement s = ut + ½at² — see the integral\'s value.
x is time t (s). The first graph is the distance fallen h = ½gt², the second the speed v = gt.
R = radius, ω = angular speed, T = time (press ▶ to move). One arrow is the velocity (along the tangent), the other the centripetal acceleration.
x is time. The graphs are displacement, velocity and acceleration. Acceleration always points against displacement, and speed is greatest where displacement is zero.
b = damping constant. The amplitude falls as A e^(−bx) — the two outer curves are that envelope.
λ = wavelength, f = frequency, T = time. Press ▶ on T and the wave moves right at v = fλ.
Press ▶ on T: the nodes never move and the antinodes swing most. Neighbouring nodes are λ/2 apart.
Adding two close frequencies makes the third graph\'s loudness rise and fall — the beat frequency is |f₁ − f₂|.
The first graph is force F = K/r², the second potential V = K/r. Double the distance: the force drops to a quarter, the potential to half. K = kq₁q₂ or GMm.
g inside and outside the Earth
x = distance from the centre (×10⁶ m). Inside, g grows with distance; outside, it falls as 1/r². It is largest at the surface (the point).
x = voltage V (volt), y = current I (ampere). The slope is 1/R.
x = time. After τ = RC the charging voltage reaches 63.2% of its final value (the point); while discharging 36.8% is left.
x = time (milliseconds). V₀ = peak; the straight line is V_rms = V₀/√2 (220 V, 50 Hz in Bangladesh).
a = (a₁, a₂), b = (b₁, b₂). The second arrow starts at the head of the first; the third is the resultant a + b (triangle law).
The arrows show the field\'s direction. Make q negative and they turn towards the charge. Longer arrows mean a stronger field.
+q sits at (1, 0), −q at (−1, 0). Change c to move the equipotential line — field arrows always cross it at right angles.
The gravitational field around a planet — every arrow points to the centre and weakens with distance.
Magnetic field of a straight wire
The wire comes out of the page towards you (at the origin). By the right-hand rule the field circles anticlockwise.
Field strength away from a wire
B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2×10⁻⁷ I/r. x = distance r (m), y = B (×10⁻⁷ T). Double the distance, half the field.
Charge moving in a magnetic field (3D)
A uniform magnetic field along z (the arrow). The velocity part across the field makes a circle (radius R), the part along it pulls forward (p) — so the path is a helix. Set p = 0 for a circle.
r = mv/(qB). x = speed v, y = radius r. More speed or mass: a bigger circle; more charge or field: a smaller one.
Object and image distance for a convex lens
1/u + 1/v = 1/f. x = object distance u, y = image distance v. At u = 2f, v = 2f; for u < f, v is negative (a virtual image). The two straight lines are asymptotes.
Snell\'s law and the critical angle
x = angle of incidence (degrees). First graph: rarer to denser. Second: denser to rarer — where it stops is the critical angle; beyond it, total internal reflection. y = x is for comparison.
d = slit separation (mm), D = screen distance (m), λ = wavelength (nm). x = position on the screen (mm), y = intensity. Fringe width β = λD/d.
a = slit width (mm). The central bright band is twice as wide as the others. A narrower slit spreads the pattern out.
I = I₀ cos²θ. x = angle between polariser and analyser (degrees). At 90° no light gets through.
N = N₀e^(−λt). The point is the half-life T½ = ln2/λ, when half the atoms are left. A larger λ decays faster.
x = frequency (×10¹⁴ Hz), y = maximum kinetic energy (eV), W = work function. The slope is Planck\'s constant h; the point is the threshold frequency — below it no electrons come out.
1 mol of gas: x = volume (L), y = pressure (kPa). The two curves are at T and 2T — the hotter one lies higher.
x = temperature (°C), y = volume (L). Extended, the line reaches zero volume at −273.15°C — absolute zero.
x = time (minutes), y = temperature (°C). The object cools towards the room temperature Tₛ (the straight line).
x = load (N), y = extension (cm). The spring constant is k = 1/slope (N/cm).
x = voltage (V), y = current (A). Resistance R = 1/slope. r and R² show how close the readings are to a line.
x = length L (m), y = period T (s). The power fit T = aL^b gives b ≈ 0.5, since T = 2π√(L/g). From a: g = 4π²/a².
x = time (hours), y = counts. The exponential fit N = N₀e^(bx) gives the decay constant λ = −b and half-life ln2/λ.
This fit doesn\'t work for this data (an exponential fit needs positive y, for example)
